title: Experiences to Issues to Actions: Developing as a Reflective Mathematics Teacher ve-mathematics-teacher/
author: Chris Shore
summary: Chris Shore, a Senior Enterprise Fellow and PhD student who tutors on the Mathematics PGCE at Loughborough University, argues that reflective practice is what allows teachers to sustain a demanding career like secondary teaching over the long term - distinguishing genuine reflection from both pure disciplinary knowledge-building and mere anecdote-collecting. Drawing on Donald Schon's classic distinction between the 'high hard ground' of technical problems solvable through research-based theory and the 'swampy lowland' of messy, confusing problems that defy technical solution, Shore argues that neither domain knowledge alone nor unreflective daily experience alone is sufficient for professional growth - genuine reflective practice integrates the two. He surveys established models of reflective practice used with PGCE trainees, including Kolb's four-stage Experiential Learning Cycle (concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation) and Gibbs' six-stage Reflective Cycle (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan), framing these as practical structures teachers of any experience level can apply to turn classroom experiences into deliberate professional development, rather than simply repeating the same year of teaching over and over.
points: Shore's opening framing: reflective practice is what separates a teacher who experiences '20 different years in school' from one who experiences 'one year repeated 20 times' - the mechanism for sustaining growth over a long career.

Drawing on Donald Schon, Shore distinguishes the 'high hard ground' of technical problems solvable through research-based theory from the 'swampy lowland' of messy, confusing problems that defy technical solution - arguing genuine expertise requires navigating both.

His key claim: reflective practice is neither pure disciplinary knowledge-building nor mere anecdote-collecting from the working day, but the deliberate integration of professional knowledge with lived classroom experience.

He introduces Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle (concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation) as one established structure PGCE trainees use to formalise reflection.

He introduces Gibbs' Reflective Cycle (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan) as a second, more granular model, illustrating that there is no single correct way to structure reflective practice - only that it must be structured.
quotes: We believe that one way to do this is by developing as a reflective teacher, so that each year is different from the last.
In fact, the joke often goes that the best teacher experiences 20 different years in school rather than just one year repeated 20 times!

In the varied topography of professional practice, there is a high hard ground overlooking a swamp. On the high ground, manageable problems lend themselves to solution through the application of research-based theory and technique. In the swampy lowland, messy, confusing problems defy technical solution.

So, thinking about your domain of knowledge (the hard high ground) is a useful practice to develop, and one of the key ways that we learn new ideas and skills. But on its own, it may not be sufficient to make progress in your chosen field.
There are almost as many models of reflective practice as there are reflective practitioners!
Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle lists four stages to effective reflection: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation.
